claims.text: The page at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ exists (link target of the 'Provider support policy' card on the support index page).
The Pulumi docs page /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ describes how long Pulumi maintains each provider major version and which providers receive long-term security updates.
Pulumi does not automatically roll back changes made during an update if an error or failure occurs; it completes pending operations in progress, then exits and reports the error.
To perform a manual rollback after a failed deployment, revert the code and configuration changes and run `pulumi up` to return infrastructure to its previous state.
Pulumi does not automatically query the cloud provider's live state before running `pulumi up` or `pulumi preview`; it compares the desired state in the program against the last recorded state.

Not refreshing automatically before every update is an intentional Pulumi design decision because refreshing requires a round-trip to the cloud provider for every resource in a stack, adding significant latency for large stacks.
Running `pulumi refresh` synchronizes Pulumi's recorded state with the actual state of cloud resources.
`pulumi up --refresh` refreshes state and applies the desired state in a single step.
Pulumi Cloud provides built-in drift detection for automated drift detection and remediation on a schedule.
The page /docs/iac/concepts/state-and-backends/ has a section 'Refreshing state' explaining refresh behavior.

In Pulumi, the logical name is part of the auto-assigned resource URN and needs to be unique only within a stack, while the physical name is how the resource is known to the cloud provider and typically must be unique within a certain scope.
Pulumi auto-naming creates each resource's physical name by combining the logical name with a random suffix appended afterwards, e.g. `my-bucket-d7c2fa0`.
Pulumi auto-naming allows Pulumi to replace resources with less downtime by creating the replacement before deleting the old resource.
Auto-naming can be disabled on a per-resource basis in Pulumi.
Project or stack configuration can be used to customize or disable auto-naming globally, per provider, or per resource type.
The page /docs/iac/concepts/resources/names/ has an 'Auto-naming Configuration' section (#autonaming-configuration) and an #autonaming section.
During a Pulumi update, secrets are decrypted in memory and visible to the Pulumi program.
Passing `--secret` to `pulumi config set` encrypts the value so it can be safely persisted in `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml`.
Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key for every stack and uses it to encrypt secrets for that stack; this is configurable to use a custom secrets provider.

Because a different key is used per stack, encrypting the same value in two stacks produces different encrypted strings in the `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` files, so an encrypted value cannot be copied between files with a text editor and `pulumi config set` must be used instead.
When running preview, update or destroy, Pulumi decrypts secret data, which is plain text during deployment execution and accessible to any part of the program via the Pulumi config object.
Pulumi does not use the Terraform engine in any way.
Some Pulumi providers use the open-source Terraform schemas to determine available resources, parameters, and return and response attributes.
Pulumi native providers are mapped directly to cloud provider APIs and do not use Terraform schemas.
Pulumi is a declarative tool that uses imperative languages to define the end state; the language is used for authoring the program and not for talking to the cloud provider API.
Pulumi uses strongly typed languages that support IntelliSense and the Language Server Protocol, so users rarely need to leave their IDE when defining Pulumi programs.
Pulumi experimental features are always opt-in, enabled explicitly with a flag, command, or environment variable such as `PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true`.
Pulumi experimental features are not necessarily supported and can change or be removed at any time without a deprecation cycle.
Pulumi focuses on actively supporting the latest released major version of the providers it maintains.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi also ships security updates for the previous major version for up to a year, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The provider support policy page lists the covered providers and what a long-term support release contains.
Pulumi-maintained provider major versions older than the previous major (and non-covered providers' older majors) receive no patches at all.
The Pulumi Registry lists the current version for all providers maintained by Pulumi.
Major provider versions typically include significant changes such as deprecations, new resources and new functionality that may require migration steps.
Minor provider versions typically include new resources, features, performance improvements and bug fixes without breaking changes.
In npm, the tilde operator (e.g. ~1.2.3) allows patch updates on the current minor version.
Patch versions of providers are primarily for bug fixes and security updates and are designed to be fully backward compatible.

Each major version of a Pulumi provider includes migration logic to smooth the upgrade from the immediately previous major version, but these migrations do not always work across multiple major versions.
Users should never be 2 major provider versions behind.
The page /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ exists (Provider support policy).
Pages /docs/support/faq/secrets-config/, /docs/support/faq/pulumi-cloud/, and /docs/support/faq/policies/ exist as the ESC, Pulumi Cloud, and Policies FAQs.
Pulumi actively maintains the latest released major version of every provider it publishes.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version (N−1) for up to 12 months, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions are AWS, Azure Classic, Azure Native, Azure AD, Command, Docker Build, GCP, Kubernetes, TLS, and Vault.
The Pulumi Registry has package pages at /registry/packages/aws/, azure, azure-native, azuread, command, docker-build, gcp, kubernetes, tls, and vault, which the LTS provider list links to.
The Pulumi provider LTS branch ships High/Critical CVE security patches, including fixes for CVEs affecting the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
The Pulumi provider LTS branch includes fixes for broken internal infrastructure on the LTS branch needed to ship the security patches.

A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain new upstream API versions, new resources or new resource properties, performance improvements, non-security bug fixes, or compatibility with newer versions of language runtimes.
Pulumi LTS provider releases remain compatible with the version of the Pulumi engine they were frozen at, unless security fixes require otherwise.
Under the Pulumi provider support policy, exactly one long-term support major version exists per provider at any time.

Under the Pulumi provider support policy, when major version N+1 ships, it becomes the new N and the old N becomes the new LTS major, and the previous LTS major reaches end of life on the same day, regardless of how much of its 12-month window remained.
Within the Pulumi provider LTS major version, only the latest minor version receives patches and earlier minor versions are frozen.
Pulumi provider LTS releases are available through the same standard package registries as current-major releases, but are tagged differently.
Customers pinning to a specific major version of a Pulumi provider (which is recommended) automatically receive patch releases as they ship.
At any time exactly one major version of a covered provider is the LTS version, and older majors receive no patches; if v3 is the latest release, v2 is N−1 (LTS) and v1 and earlier are end of life.
The current major version (N) of a Pulumi provider receives new features, new resources, bug fixes, security patches, dependency upgrades, and new upstream API versions until N+1 ships.
The LTS (N−1) version of a Pulumi provider receives security updates in the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
Pulumi provider versions N−2 and older are end of life and are not supported and will not receive updates.
The page /docs/support/faq/infrastructure/ contains a section 'What are the best practices for maintaining provider versions'.
The pages /registry/ (Pulumi Registry) and /docs/support/getting-support/ (Getting support) exist.
